endorsements.quote: Comparativeeffectiveness studies should benchmark AI systems against certified human interpreters on clinical-communication accuracy, shared-decision-making scores, visit length, cost-utility, and performance in simulated high-stakes scenarios24– 26.

Mixedmethods studies should capture how patients with NELP perceive and trust these tools, such as combining post-visit patient experience surveys with qualitative interviews, near-real-ti me smartphone experience-sampling, and multilingual sentiment analysis.

Early assessments should examine ease of use, learnability, efficiency within clinical workflows, perceived usefulness among clinicia ns and patients, acceptability, taskcompletion error rates, and integr ation with existing communication practices.

Fifth, equity-focused implementation science, includ ing interrupted time-series analyses of quality metrics and geographically diverse pragmatic studies, must evaluate whether AI interpreter services narrow or widen disparities in adverse events, readmissions, and patient-reported outcomes24,25,30.
Establishing community advisory boards of patients with NELP, professional interpreters, and cultural brokers can ensure that system development reflects community needs.
Without careful eva luation of these novel technologies ’ performance across languages and cultural contexts, they risk increasing communication-based disparities in clinical encounters.

unlisted_practices: Establish continuous error monitoring of AI interpretation using human-in-the-loop annotation pipelines in which bilingual clinicians flag clinically significant mistranslations.
Implement real-time confidence scoring that escalates uncertain AI interpretation outputs to live interpreters.
Deploy EHR-embedded safety dashboards tracking usage, error type, and override rates for AI interpreter tools.
Establish health-system oversight councils with diverse representation and authority over high-risk AI deployments.
Advocate for modality-neutral interpreter reimbursement to prevent premature substitution of certified interpreters with AI.

Limit AI language tools to low-risk written translation, commonly supported languages when certified interpreters are unavailable, temporary support pending live interpreter connection, and rare languages, and evaluate them for accuracy, safety, and patient acceptability.
Do not replace trained interpreters with AI tools that have not been validated in high-stakes clinical settings.
Develop clear metrics and methodology to assess the accuracy of AI-based interpretation.
Stratify evaluation outcomes of AI interpreter tools by language, health-literacy level, and socioeconomic status.
Include professional medical interpreters' perspectives in discussions and evaluation of AI interpreter services.

screen.reason: This is a commentary/perspective establishing a patient-centered research agenda for AI interpreter services in healthcare.
